meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Sleep, those little slices of death — how I loathe them'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Poe. No record in Poe's works; it spread via a Nightmare on Elm Street 3 title card (1987). A 1959 film villain says 'I hate those little slices of death.'

answer.label: Not Edgar Allan Poe — origin unknown; a similar 1959 film line exists
answer.authorDates: Origin untraced · a similar line is spoken in a 1959 film
answer.sourceLine: Poe never wrote this. No record of it exists in his works, and the Poe credit spread mainly from a title card in A Nightmare on Elm Street 3 (1987). The closest older wording we could find is film dialogue. In Journey to the Center of the Earth (1959), the villain Count Saknussemm says, “I don’t sleep. I hate those little slices of death.” The popular “how I loathe them” version was possibly adapted from it; no source has been traced.

source.excerpt: I don’t sleep. I hate those little slices of death.
trail: Wikiquote’s Poe page lists “Sleep. Those little slices of death. How I loathe them.” under Misattributed. It says the Poe credit comes “primarily” from a title card in A Nightmare on Elm Street 3, and that there is no record of Poe ever saying it. Wikiquote: Edgar Allan Poe ↗

The Poe Museum in Richmond, writing in 2014, says it could not trace the quote, notes that the film credited it to Poe, and concludes that it is not a Poe quote. Poe Museum: Did Poe Really Say That? ↗

The same Poe Museum post points to the 1959 film Journey to the Center of the Earth as a possible source. Wikiquote transcribes Count Saknussemm’s line there as “I don’t sleep. I hate those little slices of death.” Wikiquote: Journey to the Center of the Earth (1959) ↗

In March 2014 a Wikiquote editor proposed listing the line as a false attribution, noting that it is “widely attributed to Poe, possibly because Nightmare on Elm Street 3 claimed so.” Wikiquote: Talk page ↗
source.excerptNote: Dialogue as given on Wikiquote’s page for the 1959 film. The popular “Sleep, those little slices of death — how I loathe them” wording does not appear here. The Poe Museum relays a suggestion that it may derive from this line.

source.rightsNote: The popular “how I loathe them” wording has no identified source, so we assert no copyright status for it. The closest documented line comes from a 1959 film (20th Century Fox), well after the pre-1931 public-domain cutoff, so it should not be treated as public domain. It is not a Poe text either, so Poe’s public-domain status does not cover it.

author.name: Edgar Allan Poe
author.kicker: The name it gets pinned on
author.heading: The writer it gets pinned on
author.metaLine: 1809–1849 · American poet, short-story writer and critic
author.bio: Edgar Allan Poe (1809–1849) wrote “The Raven” and tales of horror and detection, and his image as a poet of death and sleepless nights makes him a natural home for morbid lines he never wrote. This is one of them: it is not in his writings, and the Poe Museum in Richmond, Virginia, says it is not a Poe quote. The credit spread mainly from a title card in a 1987 horror film.

misattribution.heading: How Poe got the credit
misattribution.intro: This line is pinned to Poe on quote sites, posters and social media. The attribution runs through two films and none of Poe’s own writing.

items.why: No record of the line exists in Poe’s works. Wikiquote lists it under Misattributed, and the Poe Museum says it is not a Poe quote. Poe Museum ↗

items.why: According to Wikiquote, the Poe attribution comes “primarily” from a title card in this film. That made a horror-franchise epigraph about sleep the main source for the “Poe” version. Wikiquote ↗

misattribution.truthLine: Poe did not write it. The “slices of death” image appears as film dialogue in Journey to the Center of the Earth (1959) Wikiquote: 1959 film ↗, and the Poe credit spread from A Nightmare on Elm Street 3 (1987). Wikiquote: Misattributed ↗

context.heading: Why it sticks to Poe
lead: The line sounds like Poe: it is morbid, insomniac and a little theatrical, and it matches the popular image of him as a writer of death and sleepless nights. That fit is what makes an unsourced line easy to believe, and it is why Poe attracts so many lines he never wrote.

A Nightmare on Elm Street film is about characters who dare not fall asleep, so a Poe-credited epigraph about hating sleep gave the line a natural stage. Since then the “how I loathe them” version has been copied onto quote sites without any citation to a Poe work.
context.pull: I don’t sleep. I hate those little slices of death. — Count Saknussemm, 1959
